Famous
fā´mus
adj. (renowned; rendering Hebrew shem, a name)
From Latin fama, report. The Hebrew idiom is men of name — renown as a name that travels ahead of a person.

Biblical Definition

Famous means renowned. Genesis says of the pre-flood world, “there were giants in the earth in those days… mighty men which were of old, men of renown” (Gen 6:4). Numbers calls Korah's company “famous in the congregation, men of renown” before the earth swallowed them (Num 16:2). Ruth's neighbours bless Boaz, “do thou worthily in Ephratah, and be famous in Bethlehem” (Rut 4:11), and the psalmist says of the temple's destroyers, “A man was famous according as he had lifted up axes upon the thick trees” (Psa 74:5).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines famous as celebrated in fame or public report; renowned; much talked of and praised; distinguished in story.

expand to see more

FAMOUS, a. Celebrated in fame or public report; renowned; much talked of and praised; distinguished in story.

2. Sometimes in a bad sense; notorious.

Key Scripture

Gen 6:4 — "There were giants in the earth in those days; and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare children to them, the same became mighty men which were of old, men of renown."

Num 16:2 — "And they rose up before Moses, with certain of the children of Israel, two hundred and fifty princes of the assembly, famous in the congregation, men of renown:"

Rut 4:11 — "And all the people that were in the gate, and the elders, said, We are witnesses. The LORD make the woman that is come into thine house like Rachel and like Leah, which two did build the house of Israel: and do thou worthily in Ephratah, and be famous in Bethlehem: do"

Psa 74:5 — "A man was famous according as he had lifted up axes upon the thick trees."

Modern Corruption

Renown is treated as evidence of worth, and Numbers 16 introduces the men who led the rebellion as famous in the congregation.

expand to see more

Numbers 16:2 names the credentials before the catastrophe: they rose up before Moses, with certain of the children of Israel, two hundred and fifty princes of the assembly, famous in the congregation, men of renown. These were not marginal malcontents. They were the recognized leadership, and the chapter records the ground opening under them. Fame within a religious community is not a certificate of standing before God.

Ruth 4:11 shows the word used well, and the blessing is domestic: the LORD make the woman that is come into thine house like Rachel and like Leah… and do thou worthily in Ephratah, and be famous in Bethlehem. Boaz's renown is wished for him in a village, attached to worthy conduct and a marriage. Three generations later that village produced David, and the blessing was answered more largely than anyone standing in the gate could have known.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shem (H8034), name, renown — the idiom anshe hashem, men of the name; qara shem, to call a name, in Ruth 4:11.

expand to see more

Hebrew anshe hashem — men of renown; Genesis 6:4, Numbers 16:2.

Hebrew shem (H8034) — name, fame; Ruth 4:11, 14, Genesis 11:4, let us make us a name.

Hebrew yada (H3045) — to be known; Psalm 74:5 in the sense of being noticed.

Usage

"“Famous in the congregation, men of renown” — introduced before the ground opened."

"“Be famous in Bethlehem” — renown wished in a village, answered in David."

"“Men of renown” — the pre-flood world's estimate of itself."
